ui.title: The Twelve Apostles of Jesus
ui.desc: A novel based on Part IV of The Urantia Book: the four years beside Jesus seen through the eyes of the twelve, in 26 illustrated chapters, by Jay Han.
ui.og_title: The Twelve Apostles of Jesus — The Life of Jesus Through Their Eyes
intro.title: The Twelve Apostles of Jesus
intro.sub: by Jay Han · A novel based on Part IV of The Urantia Book
intro.kick: The Life of Jesus Through Their Eyes
intro.one: From the day they were called to the day of Pentecost, the life of Jesus retold through the eyes of the twelve men who walked beside him for four years: a novel based on Part IV of The Urantia Book, with a newly painted color illustration for each of its twenty-six chapters.
intro.alt: Jesus ordaining the twelve apostles in the hills
intro.meta1: English edition · 298 pages · Five parts and an epilogue, twenty-six chapters · 26 color illustrations
intro.about1: Paper 139 of The Urantia Book paints each of the twelve apostles like a portrait: his age and family, his duties, and the strengths and weaknesses of his character. This novel begins from those portraits and walks again, through their eyes, the four years they spent beside Jesus.
intro.about2: The first five called beside the Jordan, the day six chose six, the ordination in the hills, the Galilean spring and the roads through foreign lands, the last week in Jerusalem and the denial beside the charcoal fire, the empty tomb and the confession of Thomas, and at last Pentecost. In each chapter two or three apostles stand at the center, showing in turn how Jesus and their companions looked to them, and what was in their own hearts.
intro.about3: Events, dates and places, and who did and said what, follow the text, and no words of Jesus have been invented. What is imagined is the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings and the small scenes along the road. Each chapter closes with “Sources for This Chapter,” which shows where the text ends and imagination begins.
intro.list1.title: Who This Book Is For
intro.list1.1: Readers of Part IV of The Urantia Book who want to know the apostles more closely
intro.list1.2: Readers of The Life and Teachings of Jesus who want to see the same story again from the disciples’ place
intro.list1.3: Anyone who wants to see how ordinary people walked on to the end, and to find their own face in that story
intro.pre1: This book is a novel built on The Urantia Book. Part IV of that book, “The Life and Teachings of Jesus,” tells the life of Jesus of Nazareth down to dates and places. Within it, Paper 139 paints a portrait of each of the twelve apostles: his age and family, his duties, his strengths and weaknesses, and what he most admired in Jesus. This novel began there. The longer I studied those faces, the more I wanted to walk their four years beside Jesus through their eyes.
intro.pre2: So this book follows the apostles rather than Jesus. It moves in order of time, from the first calling beside the Jordan to Pentecost. In each chapter two or three apostles stand at the center, and the story turns between them, showing Jesus, their companions, and their own hearts as each of them saw it.
intro.pre3: Events, places, dates, and who said and did what follow The Urantia Book. I have invented no events and no words of Jesus that the text does not give. His words are retold according to their sense rather than quoted, because this book cannot take the place of The Urantia Book, and I hope readers will return to the text itself.
intro.pre4: Still, this is a novel, and some of it is imagined: the apostles’ thoughts, memories, and feelings; the wind off the lake and the light of a lamp; brief exchanges among the apostles; small scenes of meals and the road. These make up roughly a third of the whole. So that readers can tell where the text ends and imagination begins, each chapter closes with “Sources for This Chapter,” giving the references behind its events and the kinds of fiction added.
intro.pre5: The book has five parts and an epilogue: Part One, The Calling; Part Two, Galilean Spring; Part Three, Foreign Lands and the Mountain; Part Four, Toward Jerusalem; Part Five, Resurrection and Pentecost; and an epilogue in which the eleven scatter. Small scenes planted early return later, so it may help to remember the fire in the garden on the night of ordination, and the hands laid on each man’s head.
intro.pre6: Why the twelve apostles? Because they were ordinary men. Fishermen with cracked hands, a steward good at figures, a despised tax collector, a Zealot who had carried a sword in his heart, a stone mason who doubted everything, and twins who understood perhaps half of the Master’s deeper sayings. Jesus entrusted his work to such men. They misunderstood, quarreled, and fell. One of them denied him at a servant girl’s word, and another said he would not believe until he saw the proof. And yet eleven of them walked on to the end. That ordinariness, I think, is the most astonishing part of the story, for what happened to them can happen to us.
intro.pre7: “What was poured into those ordinary vessels was never ordinary.”
intro.pre8: I have written the story of Judas Iscariot in sorrow. He was not a villain from the start. He was able, and his companions loved him. But he brooded over his disappointments, kept his heart shut, and slid little by little into self-deception. To the very end Jesus treated him exactly as he treated the others. Rather than hate him, I hope readers will grieve with me that such unwavering love never reached him. That, too, is a way of looking into ourselves.
intro.pre9: If, reading this book, you find your own face in one of the twelve, and remember the hands of the one who never gave that man up, then this novel will have done its work.
ch01.title: Five Men by the Jordan
ch01.b002: From early morning the camp of John below the hills of Pella smelled of smoke. In late February the Jordan valley was cold by night and quickly warm by day. It was Saturday, February 23, A.D. 26, a Sabbath morning, and on that morning a man came down out of the hills. It was Jesus of Nazareth, who had not been seen for several weeks. He walked in among the crowd and mingled with the people as though he had never been away. Andrew watched him from a distance. Of all the followers of John the Baptist, Andrew was the one who spoke least and thought longest, and he had been watching this man for a long time already.
ch01.b003: As the day wore on, a boy who had been playing on the slope fell and hurt himself. Jesus tended him, and then set out for the nearby village of Pella to bring the lad home to his parents. Andrew’s body moved before his mind had decided anything. He fell in beside them. The boy leaned on Jesus’ shoulder and sniffled, and Jesus shortened his stride to match the child’s. When they had left the boy safely at his home and turned back toward the camp, Andrew began, one by one, to bring out the questions he had been storing up for months. Jesus answered without hurry. Just before they reached the camp, the two men stopped for a while by the side of the road.
ch01.b004: Andrew knew what he was going to say. He had watched Jesus, he said, ever since the carpenter had come to live in Capernaum. He did not yet understand all of his teaching, but he believed that here was the new Teacher, and he had made up his mind to follow him. He wanted to sit at his feet and learn the truth about the new kingdom. He said it plainly, without ornament, the way he said everything. When he had finished, Jesus received him with warm assurance, as the first of his apostles. That day Andrew knew nothing of the number twelve. He knew only that he had been accepted.
ch01.b005: He was thirty-three, a full year older than Jesus. He had been born in Capernaum, the eldest of five children, and his father had died while Andrew was still a young man. Ever since, he had stood in the place of the one responsible: for his brother Simon and his three sisters, for the fish-drying business at Bethsaida, for the fishing he did in partnership with the house of Zebedee. When he took on a task he finished it, and when he had finished it he said nothing. He was clumsy at praising others, too. He so hated flattery that even honest praise, the kind that ought to be spoken, often stuck in his throat.
ch01.b006: As soon as they were back in the camp he went looking for his brother. Simon was one of John’s foremost disciples, and when he spoke in front of people, everyone listened. Andrew took him aside and told him what he had decided, and urged him to go to Jesus himself and offer himself for the service of the new kingdom. Simon’s eyes went wide. Ever since this man had come to work in Zebedee’s shop, he said, he had believed that God had sent him. Then his voice dropped.
ch01.b007: “But what about John? Can we just leave him? Is that right?”
ch01.b008: The brothers went at once to consult John. John was saddened at the thought of losing two of his ablest and most promising disciples, but he did not hold them back. This was only the beginning, he told them; his own work would soon be over, and they would all become disciples of this man. Andrew then drew Jesus aside and told him that his brother wished to join them. Jesus welcomed Simon as his second apostle. With a smile he told him that his enthusiasm did him credit but could be a danger to the work of the kingdom, and that he should learn to be more thoughtful in his speech. And from now on, he said, he would call him Peter, the rock. Simon laughed, his face reddening. Andrew could see that his brother liked the name. He could also see that his brother had already half forgotten the warning that came with it.
ch01.b009: The parents of the injured boy had begged Jesus to spend the night in their house, and he had promised. Before he left the brothers, he told them that early the next morning they would set out for Galilee.
ch01.b010: The Brothers Back from the Hills
ch01.b011: After sunset, while Andrew and Peter sat by the fire talking about the kingdom that was coming, two men walked into the camp. They were James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Dry grass seed and dust clung to the hems of their cloaks. For many days they had been scouring the hills for Jesus, and they were coming back without having found him.
ch01.b012: Peter, glad to see them, poured everything out at once. He and his brother had been received as the first associates of the new kingdom, he said, and tomorrow they were leaving for Galilee with their new Master. As John listened, he felt something drop in the middle of his chest. He was twenty-four. He and his brother James had known Jesus longer and better than anyone: in Capernaum, in their father’s boatshop, in all the large and small affairs of that household. And while they had been wandering the hills in vain, others had been chosen first.
ch01.b013: John knew that what he felt was jealousy. He knew it and could not stop it. He was the youngest of his father’s family, and the youngest child usually grows up believing he is, in some small way, special. Tonight that specialness had come to nothing. His brother James said nothing at all. James’s silences were usually either the calm before a storm or some deep thought whose reason no one could guess, and tonight even John could not tell which it was. The two of them asked where Jesus had gone and hurried off toward Pella.
ch01.b014: When they reached the house, Jesus was asleep. They woke him. Whenever John remembered it afterward, his face burned. They had shaken a sleeping man awake, and the first thing out of their mouths was a grievance. They had lived with him so long, they said, and had been searching the hills for him all this time; how could he prefer others before them?
ch01.b015: Jesus sat up. A single lamp lit the room dimly. He told them first to quiet their hearts. Then he told them to ask themselves who had sent them to go looking for the Son of Man while he was about his Father’s business. The brothers told him at length about their days in the hills: nights spent sleeping in clefts of rock, empty caves, questions put to shepherds. Jesus heard them out. Then he told them that the secret of the kingdom was not to be looked for in the hills but in their own hearts. What they had been seeking had been in their souls all along. They were truly his brothers, he said. They had never needed to be received by him at all.
ch01.b016: Still John could not keep from asking. Would he and James, then, be his associates in the new kingdom, as Andrew and Simon were?
ch01.b017: Jesus reached out and laid a hand on the shoulder of each. It was a carpenter’s hand, a hand that had built boats. John would remember its weight for a long time. Jesus told them that they had been with him in the spirit of the kingdom before they asked, before anyone else had asked. Others might go before them in the eyes of men, but in his own heart he had counted them among the councils of the kingdom before the thought of asking had even occurred to them. Indeed, if they had not taken on themselves a well-meant but self-appointed task, the search for someone who had never been lost, they would have been first before men as well. So in the kingdom to come they were not to dwell on the things that bred anxiety, but to set their minds always on doing the will of the Father in heaven.
ch01.b018: Someone who had never been lost. At those words John’s breath caught. They had not been looking for a lost man. They had gone far away to look for someone who had been beside them from the start. They had not been passed over because anyone had taken their place; they had left the place empty themselves and walked away from it. And yet this man did not scold them. Instead he told them that they had been in his heart from the beginning.
ch01.b019: John bowed his head. His eyes stung. Beside him he felt his brother’s shoulder tremble a little. The youngest son’s hurt melted under that hand. It did not vanish completely; that hidden conceit would stay with him for many years. But from that night on, the sons of Zebedee were never again envious of Andrew and Simon. And from that day the word apostle came to mark out Jesus’ chosen circle from the great company of believers who would follow him later.
ch01.b020: Late that night the four of them went together to see John the Baptist. There were tears in the prophet’s eyes, but his voice did not waver. The stalwart Judean gave up two of his leading disciples to be apostles of the Galilean Prince of the coming kingdom. Andrew looked at his face and thought: so this is what a man looks like when he gives something away.
ch01.b022: The next morning, Sunday, February 24, Jesus took leave of John by the river near Pella. The water ran brown and swollen with the winter rains, and the reeds at its edge lay bent over in the wind. The four apostles were not close enough to hear what passed between the two men. They saw only that the two stood facing each other for a long time. It was the last time either would see the other in the flesh. No one there knew it that day. Or perhaps one of them did.
ch01.b023: As they left, the camp of John was in an uproar. The day before, John had told Andrew and a disciple named Ezra, in so many words, that Jesus was the Deliverer. Andrew had acted on it; Ezra had refused. The Son of Man, Ezra declared loudly to anyone who would listen, was to come on the clouds of heaven in power. How could a Galilean carpenter be the Deliverer? Their teacher, out of sheer kindness of heart, had been deceived. When John rebuked him, Ezra drew away with a large number of disciples and went off south. Andrew looked back at that departing band as he left. Two men had heard the same words on the same day, and now they were walking in opposite directions. What was it that carried one man this way and another that way? He held on to that question for a long time. Years later it would come back to him wearing another face.
ch01.b025: Nathaniel sat in the shade of a mulberry tree by the roadside. He was on his way down from Cana with his friend Philip. They meant to find John at Pella and hear for themselves the reports that the kingdom of God was coming. While Philip went on ahead to greet some people he knew, Nathaniel rested his legs. February sunlight fell through the branches in patches. He thought about John, and about the kingdom, and about the Messiah who was expected. Thinking was his oldest pastime.
ch01.b026: He was twenty-five, the youngest of seven children. His brothers and sister were married or dead, and none of them lived in Cana anymore. The care of his aged, infirm parents fell to him alone. He had meant to become a merchant, and he and Philip had gone into several ventures together. He loved books and he loved wordplay. It was his habit to sink deep into serious thought and then spring out of it suddenly with some absurd joke. And he was rather proud of his family and of his town of Cana.
ch01.b027: While he rested in the shade, Philip’s whole life was being turned over farther up the road. Before crossing the Jordan, the little company heading north into Galilee had met Philip of Bethsaida coming the other way. Philip knew Jesus, and the four apostles knew Philip well. Peter, delighted, pulled him to one side, told him that he and his brother and the sons of Zebedee had all become Jesus’ associates in the new kingdom, and pressed him to join at once. Philip was in a quandary. Without a moment’s warning, in the middle of a road, the greatest question of his life had come at him. He looked from Peter to Andrew to John and asked one thing after another. A little apart, Jesus was explaining to James the route through Galilee to Capernaum. Watching Philip’s face grow more and more rigid, Andrew finally spoke.
ch01.b029: It was just like Andrew. He never made other people’s decisions for them. He only brought them to the place where they could decide. That settled Philip. He went straight to Jesus and asked whether he should go on down to John or join his friends who were following him. Jesus’ answer was short: Follow me. With those two words Philip was filled with the certainty that he had found the Deliverer. He waved to the others to wait a moment and ran back toward the tree where his friend was resting.
ch01.b030: Philip came up out of breath, his face flushed. Farther up the road five or six men stood waiting and looking their way.
ch01.b031: “Nathaniel, I have found the Deliverer. The one Moses and the prophets wrote about, the one John has been proclaiming.”
ch01.b032: Nathaniel looked up. Where did this teacher come from? Jesus of Nazareth, Philip said, the son of Joseph the carpenter, living lately in Capernaum. The corner of Nathaniel’s mouth twisted. Nazareth. That little village just over the ridge from Cana. To a man from Cana, Nazareth had always been a joke.
ch01.b033: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”
ch01.b034: Philip did not argue. He never did. He took Nathaniel by the arm.
ch01.b036: Nathaniel got up reluctantly. Brushing the dirt from his knees, he was already composing his next joke. If a Nazareth carpenter was the Deliverer, then the wine-seller of Cana must be high priest at the very least. But when he had crossed the road and stood before the man, the joke he had prepared vanished from the tip of his tongue.
ch01.b037: The man was looking at him. He neither rebuked the doubting face nor tried to soothe it; he simply looked at it, kindly. And he said that here was a genuine Israelite, a man without deceit. Follow me, he said.
ch01.b038: Nathaniel stood frozen. A moment ago he had mocked this man’s home town. The man might have heard it or might not. Either way, what he had seen in Nathaniel was not the mockery but the honesty: the very thing Nathaniel valued most in himself and could least put forward, the temper that could not stand a lie, lying underneath his habit of judging people before he knew them. On first sight this man had read that bottom layer before anything else. All his life Nathaniel had been good at handling his thoughts with words. Now he could not find a single one.
ch01.b040: “You were right. He really is a master of men.”
ch01.b041: Then, turning back to Jesus, he said that he too would follow, if he was worthy. Jesus nodded and told him again to follow. With that one nod Nathaniel felt something inside him turn over. His pride was not wounded. Rather, for the first time, it felt as if that pride were no longer needed.
ch01.b042: So the company became six. Andrew, Peter, James, John and Philip had all known Jesus before. Only Nathaniel was meeting him for the first time. He worked it out as he walked. Five men had followed someone they had known for a long time; he had followed someone he had just met. Which of them was the bigger fool? He laughed to himself. Philip, beside him, asked what was so funny. Nathaniel said he would tell him later.
ch01.b044: They crossed the Jordan without further delay, went by way of Nain, and reached Nazareth late in the evening. When Nathaniel realized where they were, he very nearly laughed out loud. Half a day after asking whether anything good could come out of Nazareth, he was lying down under a Nazareth roof. It was the house where Jesus had grown up, and his brother Joseph took them in.
ch01.b045: That night the apostles saw something strange. Jesus went through the house, searching it corner by corner and wiping away every trace of writing he had left behind: the ten commandments and other mottoes and sayings he had once written on walls or boards. The apostles could not understand why he took such pains to erase his own handwriting. Nathaniel watched his hands working by the lamplight. Anyone who loved writing wanted his writing to last. This man wanted the opposite. And from then on they never saw him write anything except in the dust or in the sand. That fact stayed in their minds for a long time.
ch01.b046: The next morning, before they left, the new associates told Joseph and the rest of the family about the wonderful things that had been happening: the events at the Jordan, what John had said, and their own conviction that this man was the long-awaited Deliverer. The family talked it all over among themselves. Maybe Mother had been right after all, Joseph said; maybe this strange brother of theirs was the coming king. His tone was half joking, half serious. Nathaniel recognized that tone. He used it often himself.
ch01.b048: Jesus sent the apostles on ahead to Cana, since they had all been invited to the wedding of a prominent young woman of that town, Naomi. He himself meant to stop at Magdala to see his brother Jude and then pay a quick visit to his mother at Capernaum. Cana was Nathaniel’s town. He led his companions through it, chattering at every corner about whose house that was and what story belonged to this well or that one. In between, he was able to look in on his aged parents.
ch01.b049: Jesus had warned them again and again to tell no one about him until the Father’s hour should come. But they could not stop themselves from quietly spreading the joyful news that they had found the Deliverer. John remembered what had been told of the baptism, and he believed that something would be revealed at this wedding. The whole countryside was getting ready to flock to Cana for the feast.
ch01.b050: By noon on Wednesday nearly a thousand guests had gathered in Cana, more than four times the number invited. It looked less like a wedding than a reception for Jesus. He was cordial to everyone, Jew and gentile, young and old, and he gladly agreed when they asked him to lead the wedding procession. Watching him, John felt his chest swell. Today, he thought. It will be today.
ch01.b051: In the afternoon John saw that Mary’s face had clouded over. He was the one who had long handled the affairs of that family, and he was used to reading Mary’s face. Only later did he hear what had happened. Mary, with James, had gone to her son and asked at what hour and in what way he meant to make himself known. Jesus had told them only that if they loved him, they should be willing to wait with him upon the will of his Father. For hours afterward Mary was downcast; she could not understand him, she said, and asked what it could all mean. Jesus withdrew by himself for about an hour. When he came back, he was cheerful again.
ch01.b052: Just before the wedding supper Jesus called the six aside, and he spoke to them with great earnestness. They were not to think, he said, that he had come here to work some wonder to satisfy the curious or to convince those who doubted. They were here only to wait upon the will of the Father in heaven. With that, every expectation the six had been carrying was swept away. John felt a little ashamed and a little disappointed. Nathaniel, on the other hand, felt relieved. He had no wish to see any commotion break out at a feast in his own town.
ch01.b053: But near the end of the supper the wine ran out. While the guests strolled in the garden, servants were hurrying back and forth around six great stone jars that stood near the house, jars that had been filled with water for the purification ceremonies. The servants were drawing from them, pitcher after pitcher, something red. The ruler of the feast tasted it and called the bridegroom over in amazement: everyone serves the good wine first, he said, so why had he kept the best until the end?
ch01.b054: The garden quickly filled with murmuring. The apostles rejoiced, and so did Mary. They believed Jesus had at last shown his power on purpose. Peter grabbed his brother’s arm and shook it; Philip counted the jars twice. Nathaniel stood holding his cup and thought: so this is how the name of my town will be remembered.
ch01.b055: At that moment John looked for Jesus. He was standing alone in a sheltered corner of the garden. His face was not joyful. It was the face of a man deep in serious thought. When a little later he came back among the people, everyone looked at him with awe. They all believed he was the Messiah. But soon he went up onto the housetop again and stayed there a long time. John could not understand why. On this night, at this feast, the only one not rejoicing was the very one the rejoicing was about. That strange fact lodged in John’s heart.
ch01.b057: Many of the guests stayed on for the whole week of festivities. But very early the next morning, without saying goodbye to anyone, Jesus left Cana with the six. His family and friends were dismayed, and his youngest brother Jude set out to look for him. On the road to Bethsaida Jesus told them to say nothing to anyone about the water that had become wine. He also advised them, in their future work, to keep away from Sepphoris and Tiberias.
ch01.b058: The six were walking on air. They were still walking on it that evening when they gathered in the house of Zebedee and Salome. But that evening Jesus tried to make clear to them who he was, what his work on earth was to be, and how it might end. The room went cold. They could not take in what he was saying. Even Peter could not open his mouth.
ch01.b059: Andrew endured the silence. He had not understood it all either. But someone had to answer, and the eldest always stood in that place. Slowly he said a few words. Afterward he himself could not remember well what he had said. He knew only that it had reached Jesus. What stayed longest in Andrew’s ears that night was the part about how it might end. The end, already? They had not even begun. He folded those words away in the deepest place he had. It was his way never to speak of what he was not sure of, and this was the thing he least wanted to be sure of. When Jesus saw how firmly their old ideas of the Messiah held them, he sent them off to rest. As they were breaking up, Jude arrived, and Jesus walked and talked with his brother for a long time.
ch01.b060: Jesus did not sleep that night. Going out at dawn to draw water, Andrew saw the back of the man sitting at the lakeshore, wrapped in his evening cloak. It looked as though he had been there all night. Andrew did not go to him. To let a man be alone when he wished to be alone was the deepest courtesy Andrew knew.
ch01.b061: Breakfast was a cheerless meal. At the end of it Jesus gathered them around him and told them it was the Father’s will that they stay in this neighborhood for a while. John had come to prepare the way for the kingdom, so they should wait until his preaching was finished. Then he sent them back to their nets, and he himself went off with Zebedee to the boatshop.
ch01.b062: On the Sabbath, March 2, the synagogue at Capernaum was packed with people who had heard the news from Cana. Jesus gave the six apostles seats of honor, and seated his brothers James and Jude with them. He read from the scroll of Isaiah and then said only a few words: if they were patient they would see the glory of God, and so it would be with all who stayed with him and learned to do the will of his Father. The people had come expecting to see something. They went home carrying only those words.
ch01.b063: That afternoon they took a boat a short way down the shore and anchored there. Jesus told them to go on with their usual work until the hour of the kingdom came. They were to spend three hours every evening in study, and they were to tell no one about him. They were his friends now, he said; he trusted them and he loved them. There would be great joy, but they must also be ready for trouble, and the world would stumble over his words. That evening, when they had come back to land, he stood at the water’s edge and prayed. He thanked his Father for these little ones who, for all their doubts, believed; and he asked that they too might become one. Andrew heard the words for all their doubts. They were not a reproach. They were the words of someone who knew everything and took them anyway.
ch01.b065: From March to June the waiting went on. By day they cast their nets, and by night they sat at the man’s feet. There were more than a hundred evening sessions, earnest but always cheerful. Two evenings a week they studied the Scriptures together at the synagogue. There were no miracles. Truly nothing happened. Slowly the talk about Cana died down. It was said that Herod had sent spies to look into things, but Herod was more concerned with John.
ch01.b066: For Peter those four months were torture. Again and again he urged Jesus to begin preaching in Galilee while John went on preaching in Judea. Each time Jesus told him to be patient, to make progress; when the Father called, they would be none too ready. Then Peter would come to his brother. Andrew would hear out all his complaints and say a few short words, and that was usually enough to settle him. Andrew had never envied his brother’s gift for speech. He simply liked seeing his brother shine in front of people. It was only that he had never once told him so.
ch01.b067: What astonished Andrew most was the man’s naturalness. How could someone who lived so near to God be so human, so friendly? He hauled the nets with them, laughed at their jokes, and when a child came up he stopped talking and turned to the child. They called him Rabbi, but they were no longer afraid of him. That spring they learned that being friends with God could be this easy. Years later, when all the tumult was behind them, the apostles would remember these four months as the most precious of all their time with him.
ch01.b068: During those four months John saw things the others seldom noticed. He had long been the one who looked after the affairs of Jesus’ family, and so he crossed the threshold of that house in Capernaum more often than anyone. Jesus’ brother James held fast to his faith in him and came faithfully to the evening sessions. Jude, because of sickness in his family, could seldom come. And Mary grew quieter day by day. The face that had been so bright at Cana now went back to saying, over and over, that she could not understand him, could not make out what it all meant. James’s wife did much to keep up her courage. Every time John came away from that house, his heart was heavy. And at the end of that heaviness one thought always remained. A man who was going to wander without a home had made such careful provision for his mother and his brothers and sisters. He was not understood by his family, and still he would not let go of them. John turned that over for a long time. The youngest son was learning, for the first time, to feel pity for someone.
ch01.b069: Nathaniel learned something else in the evening sessions. Jesus taught them how they should regard the various groups in Palestine: Pharisees and Sadducees, Essenes and Zealots, Herodians and Samaritans. Every one of them was waiting for a deliverer of its own. Jesus said that they would seek to win them all, but would belong to none of them. Nathaniel liked that very much. Belonging to no side was usually a coward’s excuse. But from this man it sounded like a promise to take everyone in. He explained all this to Philip at great length, and when Philip had heard him out, he asked, “Then what party are we?” Nathaniel thought about it for a while. “The supper party,” he said. That much Philip understood.
ch01.b070: In the middle of June, while Jesus was at work in the boatshop, Peter came running in, out of breath. John had been arrested. Jesus laid down his tools and took off his apron. The Father’s hour had come, he said; they should make ready to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom. It was Tuesday, June 18, his last day at the carpenter’s bench. Peter gathered all his companions and left them in a grove by the shore while he went looking for Jesus, but Jesus had gone to another grove to pray. They did not see him until late that evening, when he came back to Zebedee’s house and asked for something to eat.
ch01.b071: On the Sabbath, June 22, about ten days after John had been imprisoned, Jesus again stood in the synagogue pulpit. He said that his Father’s kingdom made no distinction between Jew and gentile, rich and poor, free and slave. That kingdom would not come with armies; it was already among them. If they would only believe that the Father loved them with an infinite love, they were already in it. About a third of those who heard believed, though they could not fully grasp it; about a third quietly made up their minds to reject so spiritual a kingdom; and the last third could not follow him at all, and many of them muttered that he was out of his mind.
ch01.b072: Leaving the synagogue, Andrew looked at the faces of his five companions one after another. Peter, all eagerness. James, sunk in thought. John, head bowed as though hiding something. Philip, counting off on his fingers the points he had heard. And Nathaniel, trying not to laugh at something only he knew. Four months ago, by the Jordan, they had begun as six. Andrew did not yet know that each of these six would soon bring one more man: Matthew Levi from the customs house at Capernaum, Thomas Didymus of Tarichea, the twins James and Judas from near Kheresa, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who had been drifting about looking for work. Those names were not yet among them. The June sun was sinking low and long over the lake.
ch01.b074: The course of events follows Paper 137, “Tarrying Time in Galilee.” The Sabbath at Pella and the injured boy, Andrew’s decision and his acceptance as first apostle, Simon’s joining and his new name (137:0.1, 137:1.1–1.4); the disappointment of James and John on their return from the hills, Jesus’ answer, and the night conversation with John the Baptist (137:1.5–1.8); the farewell to John and the division caused by Ezra (137:2.1–2.2); the calling of Philip and Nathaniel (137:2.3–2.8); the night in Nazareth and the erasing of his writings (137:2.9, 137:3.1–3.2); the wedding at Cana (137:3.6–137:4.16); the evening conference at Bethsaida, the first synagogue appearance, the teaching in the boat and the prayer by the water (137:5.1–137:6.6); and the four months of waiting and the June sermon on the kingdom (137:7.1–7.14, 137:8.1–8.18) are drawn from the text. The ages, families and characters of the apostles come from Paper 139 (139:1.1–1.10, 139:2.2, 139:3.3, 139:4.1–4.9, 139:5.2, 139:5.8, 139:6.2–6.4).
ch01.b075: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of the characters; the landscape of Pella and the Jordan valley; the details of the days spent searching the hills; the joke Nathaniel prepares and his private laughter at sleeping in Nazareth; Nathaniel guiding his friends through Cana; the gestures of the apostles at the feast; and Andrew glimpsing Jesus at the lakeshore at dawn. The wine at Cana is described only as far as the apostles saw it. The text does not record what Andrew said at the Bethsaida conference, so his answer is not invented. The six names in the final paragraph look ahead to the next chapter.
ch01.b076: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
